title: NRA releases new video directed at The New York Times
text: The National Rifle Association has a new spokesperson, Dana Loesch, whose role involves delivering scripted messages rather than anything related to firearms. Loesch, previously a Fox News commentator who served the network's purposes, has become a prominent advocate for the Second Amendment, and the NRA has placed her on camera frequently. Earlier this year, Loesch and the NRA released a recruitment video titled The Clenched Fist of Truth. The video accused the political left of assassinating real news and of using issues such as homophobia, racism and sexism to suppress the views of conservative Americans. In one sequence, schoolchildren are shown on a playground shortly before Loesch says they are being indoctrinated to believe that Trump is another Hitler. The video is offensive. Civil rights activist DeRay McKesson responded on June 29, 2017: "This NRA ad is an open call to violence to protect white supremacy. If I made a video like this, I'd be in jail." The criticism did not last long. In a period with a large volume of news under the Trump administration, the video was soon forgotten, although its message was harmful and dangerous. Loesch and the NRA have now released another video, which is similarly violent and is directed at The New York Times. Loesch phrases her threats as a warning to the newspaper, which allows her to avoid accusations of direct incitement. The accusations made in the video reflect the paranoia, suspicion and resentment of Trump supporters who prefer to regard news they dislike as fake.

title: Farmers crushed by price war! Macron vows to fix France's broken food chain
text: French farmers are being squeezed dry. Now President Emmanuel Macron says enough is enough. On Wednesday he demanded changes to France's food chain to make sure farmers, battered by shrinking margins and a brutal retail price war, finally get paid fairly. His answer? A new type of contract, based on what it actually costs farmers to produce, which would require stronger producer organizations and a change in the law. It is all part of a sweeping field-to-fork review Macron promised on the campaign trail as he tried to win over farmers, a powerful constituency in French politics who are also fed up with excessive red tape. And their plight is shocking. Last year a third of farmers earned less than 350 euros ($403) a month, according to the Agricultural Mutual Assistance Association (MSA). That is a third of the net minimum wage! Macron backed a proposal from the workshops for a reversed contract that starts with farmers, then moves to food processors and finally to retailers, spreading the added value more fairly along the chain. "We should allow farmers not to rely on subsidies anymore and therefore ensure than they be paid a fair amount for their work," Macron told farmers and food industry players at the Rungis food market near Paris. Right now, prices are set by buyers tempted to push them down, leaving many farmers unable even to cover their costs. And the retailers? A majority of them proposed raising the minimum prices they can charge on products, a move they claim could help those further down the supply chain. Macron's response: he would limit it to food products, and only back it if each sector comes up with organization plans by year-end.

title: Cruz and Kasich leave race as Trump becomes last Republican candidate
text: The field is now clear for Donald Trump to become the Republican presidential nominee. Ted Cruz and John Kasich have both withdrawn from the presidential race, leaving Trump as the only remaining Republican candidate. The two candidates, whose campaigns had been unsuccessful, made their decision after Trump won the Indiana primary last night. Dr. Inderjeet Parmar, head of the Department of International Politics at City University London, says that it has exposed a deeply divided Republican party whose leadership has lost all credibility and whose conservative philosophy, which it has held dear since 1980, is in tatters. It is the leadership of both political parties that appears to have caused this realignment in US politics towards outsiders and candidates not involved in what many regard as a corrupt and broken system. Bernie Sanders, the Democratic outsider candidate, also won against Hillary Clinton last night, an unexpected result. Two weeks ago, Cruz and Kasich announced that they had made an agreement to stop Trump, but their combined efforts did not succeed. Yesterday, a Rasmussen poll showed that Donald Trump can beat Hillary Clinton in the general election, an outcome that is becoming more likely as the political establishment retreats. Sanders supporters may not support Clinton in the general election, and their anti-establishment position is in many respects closer to Trump's politics than to those of Clinton, who is a Wall Street insider. Immediately after Kasich's announcement today, the hashtag DropOutHillary began trending on Twitter.

title: Elizabeth Warren questions FBI over difference in transparency between Clinton email case and bank investigations
text: Senator Elizabeth Warren, continuing her advocacy for ordinary citizens, has written a letter to FBI Director James Comey about the bureau's transparency in the Hillary Clinton email investigation. She noted that the FBI did not apply the same transparency when it investigated the major banks. The FBI usually does not release information when there is no indictment. The bureau changed its standards for releasing information in the Clinton case, and Warren is asking why the same standard cannot be applied to Wall Street executives. The letter states: "Your recent actions with regard to the investigation of former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton provide a clear precedent for releasing additional information about the investigation of the parties responsible for the financial crisis. These new standards present a compelling case for public transparency around the fate of the FCIC referrals. If Secretary Clinton's email server was of sufficient interest to establish a new FBI standard of transparency, then surely the criminal prosecution of those responsible for the 2008 financial crisis should be subject to the same level of transparency." Warren's argument is correct. If Clinton's emails are of sufficient interest to justify releasing as much information as possible, the information on those who have been shown to have harmed millions of Americans by causing the economic collapse should be of equal interest. It should in fact be of greater interest than the Clinton investigation, which was a politically motivated pursuit. The FBI initially released information in response to several Freedom of Information Act requests from the press and sent additional material to Congress. It did not, however, send all of the material.

title: Shocking report: 9 in 10 gang rapists in Sweden have foreign origins
text: The numbers are staggering. A new report suggests that in cases of gang rape or sexual assault involving two or more attackers in Sweden, a startling 85 percent of the attackers come from a foreign origin. The site lists the rapists' names, case numbers and other details showing the attackers' national origins, where known. And it insists: "All records and documents available on this website are Swedish public records." The longest sentence for rape went to Bardiya Coen Pajouhi, who comes from an unknown country and was sentenced for aggravated rape. And will he be deported to his country of origin? No, the site says.

title: Oil war! Baghdad tells the world: stop buying Kurdish crude
text: Iraq has drawn a line in the sand. On Sunday it urged foreign countries to stop importing crude directly from its autonomous Kurdistan region and to deal in oil only with the central government. The demand, published in a statement from Prime Minister Haider al-Abadi's office, was a direct strike back at the Kurdistan Regional Government's plan to hold an independence referendum on Monday. And who is the real target? Turkey, it seems: the transit country for every barrel of crude produced in Kurdistan, which is piped to the Turkish Mediterranean coast for export. "Baghdad asks the neighboring countries and the countries of the world to deal exclusively with the federal government of Iraq in regards to entry posts and oil," the statement declared. This is no new fight. The Iraqi government has always opposed the KRG selling crude on its own and has tried again and again to block Kurdish oil shipments. Bitter, long-running disputes over land and oil are among the main reasons the KRG gives for seeking independence. The stakes are huge. Iraqi Kurdistan pumps around 650,000 barrels per day of crude from its fields, including around 150,000 from the disputed areas of Kirkuk. That is 15 percent of total Iraqi output and around 0.7 percent of global oil production. And the KRG wants more: over 1 million barrels per day by the end of this decade. Kurdish oil has been dominated by mid-sized companies such as Genel, DNO, Gulf Keystone and Dana Gas. Oil giants including Chevron, Exxon Mobil and Rosneft also have projects in Kurdistan, though mostly still at the exploration stage.

title: A shattered brain, a family torn apart, and a broken heart that began to heal
text: I knew it would be bad. The only question was how bad. I waited outside a surgical ward at Jersey City Medical Center for what felt like an eternity. Then the neurosurgeon came out, introduced herself and told me the terrifying truth: blood clots were forming in my husband's brain, the result of multiple fractures to his skull. Even after a massive operation, the swelling and pressure inside his brain were climbing to levels "inconsistent with life," she explained. To survive the night, he needed another operation. Less than 24 hours earlier, on Dec. 13, 2014, Steve, my husband and the father of our two young children, had left our Brooklyn apartment for a networking trip to Atlantic City with four colleagues. All day he texted me updates, including a goofy selfie meant to make our daughter, then 3 years old, laugh. Then, around 6 a.m., the phone rang. Two of the colleagues who had been with him in Atlantic City told me Steve had been in an accident and that I should call the emergency room. They had been with him all day. So why couldn't they explain what had happened to him? At the hospital, the horrifying picture came together piece by piece. The trauma staff told me his face was so disfigured and bruised that they struggled to determine his race. His doctors concluded he had been assaulted. (The story of his surgery, and the mystery of his injuries, was told in an article in The Atlantic last spring.) After that second brain surgery, his neurosurgeon, Dr. Lauren Schwartz, came back with devastating news: she had removed significant chunks of Steve's frontal lobe and temporal lobe, and he might never speak or function normally again.

title: Teenager argues women would not need tampons if they had self-control
text: A 19-year-old man has objected to the debate over the U.K. tampon tax because he considers tampons to be luxury items. His reasoning is not that men do not need them. In his view, women should avoid bleeding until they are able to reach a toilet, which is not how menstruation works. The statement is not satire; he holds this view, and he has a girlfriend. He said: "People are saying tampons shouldn't be taxed because they are a necessity but why can't those women just learn to control their bladders? If they are going to bleed then they should wait until they get to the toilet. It's all about self-control. If you can't control your bladder then that's not the taxpayers problem. I don't urinate everywhere and expect free nappies." The comments drew a large amount of what he describes as hate, which was to be expected. He lacks basic biological knowledge, and those who have pointed this out are correct. Ryan regards himself as a politician and an expert on politics. On his Instagram account he describes his aim as "Making the meninist movement mainstream once again." The meninist movement is essentially the men's rights movement, whose members believe that women oppress them and regard women as the source of their problems. The comments on one of his Instagram photos, posted on Sep 20, 2016, in which he said he had bumped into Brooklyn Beckham, illustrate the reaction to his views. The criticism has not stopped him from continuing to post.

title: Inside the dazzling Havana mansion where Obama will stay: 'built to impress'
text: It has survived war, revolution and even an Albanian occupation. Now this grand mansion in Havana will host U.S. President Barack Obama and his family for two nights. With U.S.-Cuban diplomatic ties restored and relations thawing, the U.S. ambassador's residence is roaring back as a center of influence on the Communist-ruled island. Built from 1939 to 1942, the two-story mansion is more than half the size of the White House, according to U.S. State Department data, and was made with the finest materials and craftsmanship of its day. Then came the fall. The United States abandoned it from 1961 to 1977, after the 1959 Cuban revolution toppled a pro-American government and Washington cut ties with Fidel Castro. The home was left to Albanian and later Swiss caretakers. Its coral limestone exterior and marble floors and columns are both imposing and inviting, said one man who lived there, comparing it to the finest U.S. ambassadorial residences in London, Paris or Buenos Aires. "This is a place that was built to impress," said John Caulfield, America's chief diplomat in Cuba from 2011 to 2014, who lived in the upstairs two-bedroom, two-bath suite with a living room. Upstairs there are four more large bedrooms with private baths, including the presidential suite. Obama, Michelle Obama, their two daughters and the first lady's mother will sleep there Sunday and Monday nights during the first visit by a U.S. president to Cuba in a remarkable 88 years. The public and working areas fill the ground floor. The State Department bought the land and built the residence as America was being pulled into World War Two and wanted the profile of a rising power. "It's really an example of soft power. You walk through that door and it impresses."

title: Lordy! Comey sets Twitter on fire, but Trump goes strangely silent
text: Former FBI Director James Comey's blockbuster congressional testimony unleashed a social media storm on Thursday, with millions of people piling in. But one voice was strangely missing: the tweeter in chief himself. President Donald Trump's usually red-hot Twitter account went dark during the three-hour hearing of the Senate Intelligence Committee. Another Trump stepped up instead. Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, live tweeted all through Comey's testimony, slamming the ex-FBI director over his version of what the president told him. Twitter had a field day with other moments too, from Comey's revelation that he broke a date with his wife to have dinner with Trump to his use of the exclamation "Lordy." And when Comey disclosed that the person who leaked his memos of meetings with Trump was a Columbia Law School professor? A stampede hit the school's website and crashed it! Here are some of the moments that set Twitter alight. Trump Jr. went after Comey's comments on whether the president was ordering him to drop the investigation of former national security adviser Michael Flynn. "Knowing my father for 39 years when he 'orders or tells' you to do something there is no ambiguity, you will know exactly what he means," he tweeted. "Hoping and telling are two very different things, you would think that a guy like Comey would know that," he concluded, adding the hashtag "give me a break". With his father's account silent, Trump Jr.'s handle shot up to become the 10th most mentioned Twitter handle in the Comey conversation, according to social media analysis firm Brandwatch. And one remark from Comey in particular had the Twittersphere buzzing.

title: U-turn! New Zealand's protectionist firebrand Peters embraces China
text: So much for the tough talk. New Zealand will build a close relationship with China, Foreign Minister Winston Peters declared on Tuesday, burying fears that his protectionist campaign rhetoric would stir up tension with a crucial trading partner. This is the 40-year political veteran who played kingmaker in October, putting the centre-left Labour Party in power after an inconclusive election left his nationalist New Zealand First party holding the balance of power. And the stakes are high. Many in China see New Zealand as a model for how the Asian giant should deal with Western countries, and President Xi Jinping last year called the depth of the bond "unprecedented". Peters, who is also deputy prime minister, laid out his stance on China for the first time since taking office in front of academics and diplomats in Wellington. "Our record of trade and economic firsts is dramatic," he told them. "New Zealand will continue to seek closer cooperation with China as both countries focus on sustainable economic development and the wellbeing of our peoples," Peters said, giving a glowing account of 45 years of diplomatic ties. Quite a turnaround! On the campaign trail Peters ran on a protectionist platform, vowing to slash immigration and rein in foreign investment, sparking fears he could anger the Asian giant, the country's top destination for goods exports. Under the previous National government, New Zealand became the first developed country to join the China-led Asia Infrastructure Investment Bank and helped bring other Western countries along, according to treasury officials. And the money is massive: trade between the two countries has grown to more than NZ$24 billion ($16.54 billion) a year, and in March New Zealand became the first Western nation to formally sign up to China's sweeping Belt and Road global infrastructure initiative.

title: US to delay cyberwar with Russia until after election
text: The Obama administration wants to begin the cyberwar together with Hillary Clinton. While the administration has repeatedly stated its intention to start a full-scale cyberwar against Russia at a "time of their choosing," the most recent reports indicate that the war is on hold at least until the presidential election in two weeks. President Obama hopes to work with Clinton, if she becomes president-elect, to launch a cyberwar that both of them support. Both have taken a strongly hawkish position on Russia, and Obama does not want to deny Clinton the opportunity to take part in the early stages of a war she would inherit. Starting a cyberwar before a Trump victory would be even less advisable, since Trump has opposed confrontation with Russia and has expressed strong doubts about the Democratic Party's "certainty" that Russia is responsible for hacks against it. Rep. Adam Schiff (D-CA), the ranking Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, says that another factor is concern about provoking Russian retaliation for such a US attack before the vote. Many Democrats are concerned that Russia could release "forged" documents to embarrass the Clinton campaign. Earlier this month, Vice President Joe Biden said that he has informed Russia of an imminent retaliatory hack and that the Obama administration will choose a time which will "have the greatest impact." Russia has denied any involvement in the hacks.

title: Homeless man appears less cheerful than usual
text: A homeless man who is normally cheerful appears to be in a low mood today, and the reason is not known. Bill McKay, 56, usually sings Born in the USA as he greets passers-by, but local residents say he does not seem to be his usual cheerful self. Local barista Julian Cook said: “He’s usually so full of life. Dancing about the place, proposing to every girl who walks past him and then laughing when they walk off. But today he’s just sat there looking bloody depressed. “I wonder why he’s in such a mood? “ Usually I’d give him a cup of coffee and a bit of cake for being so entertaining but if he’s going to just sit there looking like he wants to cry then he can sod off.” When asked why he was unhappy, McKay shook his head, said something about the government and then looked down the street with a heavy sigh. Cook added: “See. What’s funny about that?”

title: Abandoned! Rural Nepal's quake victims still waiting for help
text: Their government has failed them, so Nepalis are taking matters into their own hands. Furious at the chaotic, bureaucratic official response to the earthquake, citizens are delivering aid to victims themselves. They have hired their own trucks and crammed vehicles with plastic sheets for shelter and bags of rice and lentils for food. But with every day that passes since the magnitude-7.8 earthquake struck on April 25, this self-help effort is getting harder. Youths from various political parties are throwing up makeshift checkpoints on the roads to the hardest-hit areas, or chasing down vehicles on motorbikes along narrow, isolated mountain roads and demanding the aid be handed over to them to distribute. Such political maneuvering is nothing new, but many Nepalis are outraged. And the victims are desperate. "I have nothing left. One daughter is buried under my house. my other daughter was sent to a hospital," said Bhampagiri, 72, who lives in the hamlet of Pawachok, a two-hour drive from the capital. "I have no food. Nothing. My house has collapsed so I sit here by the road and wait hoping someone will pass and help me," said Bhampagiri, who goes by one name. Heartbreaking. And what has the government been doing? In the past week it has held up customs clearance of international aid at Nepal's only international airport in Kathmandu, and has been charging duty on truckloads of tarps brought in from India by Nepali Good Samaritans. At the same time, it has asked international donors for an additional 400,000 tents and tarpaulins, as well as blankets. The death toll has passed 7,000 and is expected to climb sharply once hard-hit remote areas are reached. This week, the airport in Kathmandu finally got some much-needed help from about 150 U.S. Marines.

Out of the middle of its division, a burning torch sprang, throwing out a long way, flames, coals, and sparks.”

title: Bernie Sanders unable to explain why single-payer was rejected in Democratic states
text: Senator Bernie Sanders, an advocate of socialized medicine, was unable on Sunday to explain why a single-payer health care system was rejected in Vermont and California, two strongly Democratic states, when he was pressed on the question. CNN host Jake Tapper said that California and Vermont are solidly Democratic states and asked how single-payer could be affordable at the national level if those states had rejected the system because of its cost. Single-payer failed to pass in both California and Vermont after lawmakers were unable to determine how to fund the system. Voters in Colorado also rejected single-payer last year. Sanders disputed Tapper's point, citing studies he has seen, and said that single-payer would save the average family significant sums of money. "If you look at Canada's single-payer health care system per capita, their costs are far far less than the United States," Sanders said. "If you look at the UK, if you look at countries around the world, all of which have different approaches to a national health care system, in every instance, they are spending substantially less per capita than we pay in the United States."

title: Revolt! Senate Democrats set to defy Obama on Saudi 9/11 bill
text: Obama's own party is turning on him. The Democratic leaders of the U.S. Senate said on Tuesday they expected the chamber to override President Barack Obama's promised veto of a bill letting relatives of victims of the Sept. 11 attacks sue Saudi Arabia. It would be the first override of an Obama veto since he took office in January 2009. A historic slap! The “Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act,” known as JASTA, would strip sovereign immunity, which shields governments from lawsuits, from countries found to be involved in terrorist attacks on U.S. soil. Remember: fifteen of the Sept. 11 hijackers who crashed airliners in the 2001 attacks were Saudi nationals. The Saudi government, which strongly denies responsibility, has lobbied hard against the bill. But patience in Congress is wearing thin, with some members increasingly restless about relations with Saudi Arabia, long a key player in U.S. Middle East policy. Harry Reid, the Senate's Democratic leader, backed the measure. And he did not mince words about the Saudis: “They’re not one of my favorite countries,” he said. Richard Durbin, the No. 2 Senate Democrat, said: “We’re all on the record supporting it, so at this point I think it’s a heavy lift for the president to have his veto sustained.” So what is the White House doing? title: Down to the wire! States scramble to save Obamacare coverage in every county
text: It came down to the bitter end. U.S. states have fought to keep health insurers selling Obamacare plans in every county next year, in some cases playing hardball to stop exits that would leave residents with no access to coverage. But nobody can rule out a last-minute pullout. Insurers must sign government contracts spelling out where they will offer 2018 coverage by midnight on Wednesday. In recent months, dozens of U.S. counties faced the frightening prospect of having no insurer offering subsidized individual coverage next year after national giants including Anthem Inc, Aetna Inc and Humana Inc announced they were pulling out. Why? Many insurers have lost money on Obamacare. Others fear being exposed to a program that President Donald Trump and the Republican-controlled Congress want to repeal. Trump has even threatened to cut billions in subsidy payments to insurers to undermine predecessor Barack Obama's healthcare law. Still, insurance commissioners in Republican-leaning states such as Tennessee, Missouri and Virginia spent months negotiating with insurers to find out who might pull out and either persuade them to stay or find a replacement. By Tuesday, it looked like they had pulled it off, keeping every county covered in every state. But consumers are not out of the woods. Nearly half of U.S. counties have no choice at all, with only one insurer selling individual plans. And many insurers have filed price hikes of 20 percent or more to cover the political uncertainty. Some states still dread a last-minute shock. “My colleagues and I are still very concerned that today insurers are making a decision about whether or not to participate,” said Tennessee insurance commissioner Julie McPeak. “That makes us nervous.”

title: Cold War chill! Trump to sign Russia sanctions as Moscow hits back hard
text: Moscow has struck back, and the gloves are off. U.S. President Donald Trump will sign legislation imposing sanctions on Russia, the White House said on Friday, after Moscow ordered the United States to slash hundreds of diplomatic staff and said it would seize two U.S. diplomatic properties in retaliation for the bill. On Thursday, the U.S. Senate voted almost unanimously to slap new sanctions on Russia, cornering Trump: take a tough line on Moscow and effectively kill his hopes for warmer ties, or veto the bill in the middle of investigations into possible collusion between his campaign and Russia. And once the bill becomes law, Trump cannot ease the sanctions without congressional approval. Moscow's retaliation, announced by the Foreign Ministry on Friday, was straight out of the Cold War. If Russia's move really does hit hundreds of staff at the U.S. embassy, it would dwarf the Obama administration's expulsion of 35 Russians in December. The legislation was partly a response to U.S. intelligence findings that Russia meddled in the 2016 U.S. presidential election, and further punishment for its annexation of Crimea in 2014. Late on Friday, the White House said Trump would sign the bill after reviewing the final version. Its statement said nothing about Russia's retaliation. Russia had been threatening this for weeks. Its response suggests it has given up its early hopes of better ties with Washington under Trump, something the U.S. leader had said before his election that he wanted to achieve. Relations were already stuck at a post-Cold War low over allegations that Russian cyber interference in the election was meant to boost Trump's chances, something Moscow flatly denies.
